profiles.meeting_scenario: A coordination meeting at a mid-sized law firm between the transactional and knowledge-management workstreams preparing a client-facing thought leadership paper titled "Clarifying Business Models: Origins, Present, and Future of the Concept" for the firm's Technology and Information Governance practice. The paper is intended to support future client conversations about platform businesses, SaaS providers, and data-driven ventures, and may later be repurposed into an internal issue map for live matters. The immediate agenda is to align on handoffs between the legal analysis and editorial/research workstreams: what the next draft should contain, which source set is considered the baseline, how the firm's eight legal propositions should be presented, and where supporting authorities and internal notes will live. The expected outcome is apparent agreement on who will circulate the next draft, what "annotated" and "finalized" mean for that handoff, and how shared research materials will be maintained over the next week.

members.name: Rachel Stein
members.expertise: Commercial technology agreements, platform governance, SaaS contracting, and translating academic concepts into client-facing legal frameworks
members.background: Rachel is a senior transactional lawyer who leads the practice group's external client alerts and often turns complex interdisciplinary topics into concise partner-ready pieces; she has worked closely with startup and enterprise software clients and is used to marking up Word drafts with embedded comments.
members.private_state: Rachel wants the paper to be polished enough for the practice chair to review by the end of the week without exposing unresolved doctrinal hedges, and she wants to minimize extra coordination overhead by keeping the drafting process in the familiar partner-review format.
hidden_assumptions: When a paper is described as the next 'draft,' it means a near-client-facing Word document with narrative prose, footnotes, and only limited visible editorial clutter.
An 'annotated' version means targeted margin comments flagging questions or authority support, not a separate research apparatus or exhaustive source mapping.
The 'eight propositions' belong in the main body as concise thesis statements that can stand on their own for client readers.
The current baseline materials are the authorities and notes already folded into the latest circulated Word draft from last Thursday, so duplicative source tracking elsewhere is unnecessary.
Once she says a section is 'finalized,' it is substantively stable enough for partner circulation even if citation cleanup continues in parallel.

members.name: Daniel Wu
members.expertise: Legal research systems, precedent curation, editorial workflow design, citation verification, and converting subject-matter outlines into reusable knowledge assets
members.background: Daniel supports multiple practice groups by structuring research memos, maintaining authority banks, and preparing publishable thought leadership materials that can later feed internal playbooks; he commonly works from shared research spreadsheets and version-controlled document folders.
members.private_state: Daniel wants this paper to become a durable internal resource, not just a one-off alert, and he is trying to ensure that all propositions and terminology are traceable to source literature before the piece reaches partner review.
hidden_assumptions: The next 'draft' should still function as a working document with visible structure, source placeholders, and enough metadata for later reuse.
An 'annotated' version means each proposition and terminology choice is linked to supporting sources in a research table or appendix, not merely commented in the margins.
The 'eight propositions' are a supporting framework best kept in an appendix or matrix so the main text stays conceptually clean.
The operative source baseline is the shared research folder and literature chart updated by the library team on Monday, even if not yet reflected in the Word draft.
A section is only 'finalized' once the authorities are checked and the proposition-to-source mapping is complete, because otherwise downstream reuse becomes unreliable.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree that Daniel will send Rachel an 'annotated draft' before partner review.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: Rachel expects a clean-ish Word draft with a manageable number of margin comments and perhaps a few footnotes added.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: Daniel intends to deliver a working package consisting of a heavily marked draft plus a source matrix showing how terms and propositions map to literature.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both regularly use the phrase 'annotated draft' in professional settings, and each version sounds normal within legal publishing workflows, so neither thinks the term needs unpacking.

misalignment_points.topic: Which materials are 'the current source set'
misalignment_points.surface_form: They refer to using 'the current source set' or 'the latest materials' when updating the paper.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: Rachel is thinking of the authorities already embedded or cited in the Word draft she last edited on Thursday.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: Daniel is thinking of the shared literature chart and article PDFs refreshed by the library team on Monday, including several sources not yet folded into the draft.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both assume the other is naturally referring to the most up-to-date body of materials, but each anchors 'latest' to the repository they personally treat as authoritative.

misalignment_points.topic: What it means for a section to be 'finalized'
misalignment_points.surface_form: They agree that the terminology and propositions sections should be 'finalized' before Rachel sends the piece up the chain.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: Rachel means the prose, structure, and practical framing are stable enough for partner circulation even if source checking continues afterward.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: Daniel means the sections are not finalized until every proposition is source-backed, citations are confirmed, and cross-references are locked.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In law-firm workflows, 'finalized' is often used loosely to mean 'ready for the next person,' and both participants are focused on coordination rather than explicitly debating readiness criteria.

misalignment_points.surface_form: They discuss 'including the eight propositions in the draft' as part of the upcoming handoff.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: Rachel assumes inclusion means integrating all eight propositions into the main narrative as short client-facing takeaways.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: Daniel assumes inclusion means ensuring the propositions are present somewhere in the deliverable, most likely in an appendix, chart, or boxed framework tied to sources.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both sincerely agree the propositions must be 'in the draft,' and the phrase does not force them to specify whether inclusion is in the article body or in supporting material.

If we can get the terminology and the eight propositions into stable prose by midweek, I can polish the body and send something that looks mature to the practice chair. For me, finalized means the sections read cleanly and the framing is settled enough for circulation, even if we are still tightening cites in the background. And including the eight propositions means they should appear in the actual article text as concise takeaways, not floating off somewhere else.
